To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the retention behavior is mab dependent and should be optimized individually, the particle size influences retention rather than efficiency and that the whole phase system should be considered when optimizing the method.

1) The retention behavior of mAbs on cation exchange stationary phases is strongly influenced by the combination of mobile phase pH and salt concentration, 2) the particle size of cation exchange stationary phase has no influence on the efficiency of the columns, 3) cation exchange columns are highly complementary in their retention and selectivity, and 4) short, narrow bore columns are very attractive for the analysis of charge variants.

The retention, selectivity, and efficiency of cation exchange chromatography applied for therapeutic monoclonal antibody separation are strongly influenced by the combination of stationary and mobile-phase composition and that the whole phase system should be considered while developing a method.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic evaluation of different cation exchange stationary phases for the separation of therapeutic monoclonal antibody variants.
the optimization of the separation of therapeutic monoclonal antibody charge variants using cation exchange chromatography.
the development and evaluation of new stationary phases and mobile phases that are able to separate charge variants of therapeutic monoclonal antibody products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the selection of stationary phase is not a trivial decision, but a very complex task, which requires a profound knowledge of the properties of the stationary phase as well as the properties of the analytes.
there is no "best" cation exchanger column for the separation of monoclonal antibodies.
the selection of the appropriate column is a key factor for the success of cation exchange chromatography in monoclonal antibody charge variant analysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there is no one column that can be used to separate all monoclonal antibodies in a single step, and the best column for a specific antibody depends on the antibody itself and the separation objective.

there is a large potential to improve selectivity, efficiency, and resolution in ion exchange separations of large biomolecules, and that it is possible to achieve this by using different combinations of stationary phase and mobile phase.
the combination of stationary and mobile-phase is crucial for the retention and efficiency of cation exchange chromatography separations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to consider the whole phase system when developing an ion exchange chromatographic method.
there is no universal cation exchange column for the separation of therapeutic monoclonal antibody charge variants.
the whole chromatographic phase system (stationary and mobile phase) has to be considered while optimizing charge variant assays.
